topic.title: FortiGate CLI
topic.description: FortiOS 7.4 CLI for what you do in the web UI: interfaces, objects, policies, routes, port forwarding and diagnostics. Each drill names the equivalent web UI page.

commands.name: config system interface
commands.synopsis:
config system interface
    edit <name>
        set <option> <value>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Network › Interfaces › (double-click an interface). Sets the IP address, alias, role and which management protocols (ping, https, ssh) the interface accepts.

flags.description: Interface address. Web UI: IP/Netmask field.
Management access list; replaces the whole list. Web UI: Administrative Access checkboxes.
Enable or disable the interface. Web UI: Status toggle.

examples.title: Set the LAN address
examples.scenario: Give port1 the address 192.168.10.1/24 (Web UI: Network › Interfaces › port1 › IP/Netmask).
examples.command:
config system interface
    edit "port1"
        set ip 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
    next
end
examples.explanation: edit enters the interface; next saves it; end leaves the config section.

examples.title: Management access
examples.scenario: Allow ping, HTTPS and SSH on port1 (Web UI: Administrative Access checkboxes).
examples.command:
config system interface
    edit "port1"
        set allowaccess ping https ssh
    next
end
examples.explanation: allowaccess replaces the full list; include every protocol you want to keep.

examples.title: Name the interface
examples.scenario: Set the alias of port1 to LAN (Web UI: Alias field).
examples.command:
config system interface
    edit "port1"
        set alias "LAN"
    next
end

use_cases.title: Locked out of the GUI
use_cases.situation: HTTPS was removed from allowaccess; restore it from the console.

pitfalls: Never remove https/ssh from the interface you are connected through.

commands.name: config firewall address
commands.synopsis:
config firewall address
    edit <name>
        set subnet <ip> <mask>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Policy & Objects › Addresses › Create New › Address. Objects are referenced by name in policies.

flags.description: Host (/32) or network. Web UI: IP/Netmask.
Resolve by DNS name. Web UI: Type = FQDN.

examples.title: Host object
examples.scenario: Create an address srv-web for host 10.0.10.20 (Web UI: Addresses › Create New › Address).
examples.command:
config firewall address
    edit "srv-web"
        set subnet 10.0.10.20 255.255.255.255
    next
end

examples.title: Subnet object
examples.scenario: Create an address net-servers for 10.0.10.0/24.
examples.command:
config firewall address
    edit "net-servers"
        set subnet 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0
    next
end

examples.title: FQDN object
examples.scenario: Create an FQDN address api-partner for api.example.com (Web UI: Type = FQDN).
examples.command:
config firewall address
    edit "api-partner"
        set type fqdn
        set fqdn "api.example.com"
    next
end

use_cases.title: New server
use_cases.situation: Create the object before writing the policy that allows it.

commands.name: config firewall addrgrp
commands.synopsis:
config firewall addrgrp
    edit <name>
        set member <addr> ...
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Policy & Objects › Addresses › Create New › Address Group. One policy can then cover many objects.

flags.description: Replaces the member list. Web UI: Members.
Adds members without retyping the list.

examples.title: Create a group
examples.scenario: Create grp-web with members srv-web1 and srv-web2 (Web UI: Address Group › Members).
examples.command:
config firewall addrgrp
    edit "grp-web"
        set member "srv-web1" "srv-web2"
    next
end

examples.title: Add a member
examples.scenario: Add srv-web3 to grp-web without removing the existing members.
examples.command:
config firewall addrgrp
    edit "grp-web"
        append member "srv-web3"
    next
end
examples.explanation: set member would replace the list; append adds to it.

use_cases.title: Scale out
use_cases.situation: A new web server joins the pool already allowed by policy.

commands.name: config firewall service custom
commands.synopsis:
config firewall service custom
    edit <name>
        set tcp-portrange <ports>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Policy & Objects › Services › Create New › Service. Built-in services (HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, DNS…) already exist.

examples.title: TCP service
examples.scenario: Create a service TCP-8443 for TCP port 8443 (Web UI: Services › Create New).
examples.command:
config firewall service custom
    edit "TCP-8443"
        set tcp-portrange 8443
    next
end

examples.title: UDP range
examples.scenario: Create a service RTP-media for UDP ports 10000 to 20000.
examples.command:
config firewall service custom
    edit "RTP-media"
        set udp-portrange 10000-20000
    next
end

use_cases.title: Application on a non-standard port
use_cases.situation: Allow only the port the application uses instead of ALL.

commands.name: config firewall policy
commands.summary: Firewall policies (who can talk to whom)
commands.synopsis:
config firewall policy
    edit <id>
        set <option> <value>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Policy & Objects › Firewall Policy › Create New. Policies are evaluated top-down; the first match wins. 'edit 0' creates a policy with the next free ID.

flags.description: Incoming and outgoing interfaces. Web UI: Incoming/Outgoing Interface.
Source NAT to the outgoing interface IP. Web UI: NAT toggle.
Log all sessions. Web UI: Log Allowed Traffic = All Sessions.
Disable without deleting. Web UI: right-click › Set Status.

examples.title: LAN to Internet (HTTPS)
examples.scenario: Allow HTTPS from lan to wan1 with NAT (Web UI: Firewall Policy › Create New).
examples.command:
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "lan-to-wan-https"
        set srcintf "lan"
        set dstintf "wan1"
        set srcaddr "all"
        set dstaddr "all"
        set service "HTTPS"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set nat enable
    next
end

examples.title: Disable a policy
examples.scenario: Temporarily disable policy 5 without deleting it (Web UI: right-click › Set Status › Disable).
examples.command:
config firewall policy
    edit 5
        set status disable
    next
end

examples.title: Reorder policies
examples.scenario: Move policy 7 above policy 2 (Web UI: drag the row in the policy list).
examples.command:
config firewall policy
    move 7 before 2
end
examples.explanation: Order matters: the first matching policy is applied.

examples.title: Log every session
examples.scenario: Make policy 5 log all sessions, not only security events.
examples.command:
config firewall policy
    edit 5
        set logtraffic all
    next
end

use_cases.title: New application access
use_cases.situation: Open exactly one service between two zones.

use_cases.title: Traffic blocked unexpectedly
use_cases.situation: A broader deny above the new policy matches first; reorder.

pitfalls: A new policy is appended at the bottom; check that no earlier policy matches first.

commands.name: config router static
commands.synopsis:
config router static
    edit <id>
        set dst <ip> <mask>
        set gateway <ip>
        set device <iface>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Network › Static Routes › Create New. 'edit 0' adds a route with the next free ID; without dst it is the default route.

flags.description: Next hop. Web UI: Gateway Address.

examples.title: Default route
examples.scenario: Send all Internet traffic to 203.0.113.1 via wan1 (Web UI: Static Routes › Create New, Destination 0.0.0.0/0).
examples.command:
config router static
    edit 0
        set gateway 203.0.113.1
        set device "wan1"
    next
end

examples.title: Route to a branch network
examples.scenario: Reach 10.20.0.0/16 through 192.168.1.254 on port2.
examples.command:
config router static
    edit 0
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0
        set gateway 192.168.1.254
        set device "port2"
    next
end

use_cases.title: New remote site
use_cases.situation: Add the route before the policy, or replies will leave by the default route.

commands.name: config firewall vip
commands.synopsis:
config firewall vip
    edit <name>
        set extip <ip>
        set mappedip <ip>
    next
end
commands.description: Web UI: Policy & Objects › Virtual IPs › Create New. Maps a public address/port to an internal server; a policy with the VIP as destination is still required.

flags.description: Public address. Web UI: External IP address.
Interface receiving the traffic. Web UI: Interface.
Internal server. Web UI: Map to IPv4 address.
Translate a port. Web UI: Port Forwarding toggle.

examples.title: Publish an internal web server
examples.scenario: Forward 203.0.113.10:443 on wan1 to 10.0.10.20:443 (Web UI: Virtual IPs › Create New, Port Forwarding on).
examples.command:
config firewall vip
    edit "vip-web"
        set extip 203.0.113.10
        set extintf "wan1"
        set mappedip "10.0.10.20"
        set portforward enable
        set extport 443
        set mappedport 443
    next
end

examples.title: Policy for the VIP
examples.scenario: Allow HTTPS from wan1 to the VIP vip-web on internal interface lan.
examples.command:
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "wan-to-web"
        set srcintf "wan1"
        set dstintf "lan"
        set srcaddr "all"
        set dstaddr "vip-web"
        set service "HTTPS"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
    next
end
examples.explanation: The destination is the VIP object, not the server's internal address.

use_cases.title: Publish a service
use_cases.situation: Expose an internal server on one public port only.

pitfalls: Without the matching policy the VIP does nothing; NAT is usually disabled on inbound VIP policies.

commands.name: config system dns
commands.summary: DNS servers used by the FortiGate
commands.synopsis:
config system dns
    set primary <ip>
    set secondary <ip>
end
commands.description: Web UI: Network › DNS. Used for FQDN objects, updates and the FortiGate's own lookups.

examples.title: Set DNS servers
examples.scenario: Use 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 as DNS servers (Web UI: Network › DNS › Specify).
examples.command:
config system dns
    set primary 1.1.1.1
    set secondary 8.8.8.8
end
examples.explanation: This section has no edit/next: it is a single global setting.

use_cases.title: FQDN objects unresolved
use_cases.situation: FQDN addresses stay empty when DNS servers are unreachable.

commands.name: show
commands.description: Prints configuration in CLI format. Web UI equivalent: the edit page of each object, or the configuration backup (admin menu › Configuration › Backup).

flags.description: Include default values, not only changed ones.

examples.title: One policy
examples.scenario: Show the configuration of firewall policy 5.
examples.command: show firewall policy 5

examples.title: Interface with defaults
examples.scenario: Show port1 including default values.
examples.command: show full-configuration system interface port1

examples.title: Search the configuration
examples.scenario: Find where srv-web is referenced in firewall policies.
examples.command: show firewall policy | grep -f srv-web
examples.explanation: -f prints the whole matching block, not just the line.

use_cases.title: Change review
use_cases.situation: Read the exact configuration before and after an edit.

commands.name: get system status
commands.description: Web UI: Dashboard › Status (System Information widget). Shows version, serial number, HA mode and more.

examples.title: Firmware version
examples.scenario: Which FortiOS version and serial number does this unit have?
examples.command: get system status
examples.output:
Version: FortiGate-60F v7.4.4,build2662,240514 (GA.F)
Serial-Number: FGT60FTK2209XXXX
Operation Mode: NAT

output_notes.anomaly: End-of-support branch or a build with known PSIRT advisories.

use_cases.title: Before an upgrade or a support ticket
use_cases.situation: Confirm the exact build and serial.

commands.name: get router info routing-table
commands.description: Web UI: Dashboard › Network › Routing widget (or the Static & Dynamic Routing monitor). Shows the routes actually in use.

examples.title: All routes
examples.scenario: Display the full active routing table.
examples.command: get router info routing-table all

examples.title: Route for one destination
examples.scenario: Which route is used to reach 10.20.0.5?
examples.command: get router info routing-table details 10.20.0.5

use_cases.title: Branch unreachable
use_cases.situation: Confirm the static route is active and not overridden.

commands.name: diagnose sys session
commands.synopsis:
diagnose sys session filter <field> <value>
diagnose sys session list
commands.description: Web UI: Dashboard › FortiView Sessions. Lists sessions in the session table; always set a filter first.

examples.title: Sessions to a server
examples.scenario: List sessions whose destination is 10.0.10.20 (Web UI: FortiView Sessions, filter by destination).
examples.command:
diagnose sys session filter dst 10.0.10.20
diagnose sys session list

examples.title: Reset the filter
examples.scenario: Clear the session filter after troubleshooting.
examples.command: diagnose sys session filter clear

use_cases.title: Is traffic passing?
use_cases.situation: Confirm sessions exist for a flow and which policy they matched.

pitfalls: Listing without a filter on a busy unit prints thousands of sessions.

commands.name: diagnose debug flow
commands.summary: Trace how the FortiGate handles a packet
commands.synopsis:
diagnose debug flow filter addr <ip>
diagnose debug flow trace start <n>
diagnose debug enable
commands.description: Shows route lookup, policy match and NAT for matching packets. No full web UI equivalent; Policy & Objects › Firewall Policy › Policy Lookup answers only which policy would match.

examples.title: Trace traffic to a host
examples.scenario: Trace 20 packets involving 10.0.10.20 with function names.
examples.command:
diagnose debug reset
diagnose debug flow filter addr 10.0.10.20
diagnose debug flow show function-name enable
diagnose debug flow trace start 20
diagnose debug enable
examples.output:
id=65308 trace_id=1 func=print_pkt_detail line=5845 msg="vd-root:0 received a packet(proto=6, 192.168.10.50:51544->10.0.10.20:443)"
id=65308 trace_id=1 func=fw_forward_handler line=881 msg="Denied by forward policy check (policy 0)"

output_notes.meaning: No policy matched; the implicit deny dropped it.
output_notes.anomaly: policy 0: create or reorder a policy.

examples.title: Stop debugging
examples.scenario: Turn debugging off and clear the filters.
examples.command:
diagnose debug disable
diagnose debug reset

use_cases.title: Why is it blocked?
use_cases.situation: Prove whether routing, policy or NAT drops the flow.

pitfalls: Always disable and reset debugging when finished.

commands.name: diagnose sniffer packet
commands.description: Web UI: Network › Diagnostics › Packet Capture (7.4; Network › Packet Capture in 7.0/7.2). Shows whether packets arrive and leave on each interface.

examples.title: Capture a flow
examples.scenario: Capture 20 packets on any interface for host 10.0.10.20 port 443, with interface names.
examples.command: diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 10.0.10.20 and port 443' 4 20 l

examples.title: Capture pings
examples.scenario: Capture ICMP on wan1 to verify ping replies.
examples.command: diagnose sniffer packet wan1 'icmp' 4 10

use_cases.title: Does it reach the firewall?
use_cases.situation: Confirm packets enter on one interface and leave on the other.

commands.name: execute ping
commands.summary: Ping and traceroute from the FortiGate
commands.description: Web UI: use the CLI Console (>_ icon at the top right). execute ping-options sets the source address.

examples.title: Ping from the firewall
examples.scenario: Ping 8.8.8.8 from the FortiGate itself.
examples.command: execute ping 8.8.8.8

examples.title: Ping from the LAN address
examples.scenario: Ping 10.20.0.5 using source 192.168.10.1, to test a route as LAN traffic.
examples.command:
execute ping-options source 192.168.10.1
execute ping 10.20.0.5

examples.title: Traceroute
examples.scenario: Trace the path from the FortiGate to 8.8.8.8.
examples.command: execute traceroute 8.8.8.8

use_cases.title: ISP down?
use_cases.situation: Test upstream reachability directly from the edge.

procedures.title: Publish an internal web server on HTTPS
procedures.context: The intranet server 10.0.10.20 must be reachable from the Internet on 203.0.113.10:443.
procedures.goal: Create the VIP and the inbound policy, then verify.

steps.command:
config firewall vip
    edit "vip-web"
        set extip 203.0.113.10
        set extintf "wan1"
        set mappedip "10.0.10.20"
    next
end
steps.purpose: Virtual IP (Web UI: Policy & Objects › Virtual IPs)

steps.command:
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "wan-to-web"
        set srcintf "wan1"
        set dstintf "lan"
        set srcaddr "all"
        set dstaddr "vip-web"
        set service "HTTPS"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
    next
end
steps.purpose: Inbound policy (Web UI: Firewall Policy › Create New)

steps.command:
diagnose sys session filter dst 10.0.10.20
diagnose sys session list
steps.interpretation: Sessions with the VIP translated to 10.0.10.20 confirm the publication works.

use_cases.title: New public service
use_cases.situation: Expose one service without opening the whole server.

procedures.title: Find out why traffic is blocked
procedures.context: Users on the LAN cannot reach 10.0.10.20:443.
procedures.goal: Prove whether packets arrive and which policy decision drops them.

steps.command: diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 10.0.10.20 and port 443' 4 10 l

diagnose debug reset
diagnose debug flow filter addr 10.0.10.20
diagnose debug flow trace start 10
diagnose debug enable
steps.interpretation: 'policy 0' means no policy matched; reorder or add one.

steps.command:
diagnose debug disable
diagnose debug reset

use_cases.title: Ticket: application unreachable
use_cases.situation: Answer with evidence instead of guessing at rules.

procedures.title: Bring up a new LAN segment
procedures.context: port3 will serve a new servers network 10.0.30.0/24.
procedures.goal: Address the interface, create the object and allow Internet access.

steps.command:
config system interface
    edit "port3"
        set ip 10.0.30.1 255.255.255.0
        set allowaccess ping
    next
end
steps.purpose: Interface address (Web UI: Network › Interfaces › port3)

steps.command:
config firewall address
    edit "net-servers2"
        set subnet 10.0.30.0 255.255.255.0
    next
end

config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "servers2-to-wan"
        set srcintf "port3"
        set dstintf "wan1"
        set srcaddr "net-servers2"
        set dstaddr "all"
        set service "ALL"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set nat enable
    next
end

procedures.title: Add and verify a route to a branch
procedures.context: The branch network 10.20.0.0/16 is reachable through 192.168.1.254 on port2.
procedures.goal: Add the static route and confirm it is active and reachable.

steps.command:
config router static
    edit 0
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0
        set gateway 192.168.1.254
        set device "port2"
    next
end
steps.purpose: Static route (Web UI: Network › Static Routes)

procedures.title: Restore lost web UI access
procedures.context: After an edit, the web UI on port1 no longer opens; you are on the serial console.
procedures.goal: Check management access on port1 and re-enable HTTPS.

steps.interpretation: https missing from allowaccess explains the lockout.

steps.command:
config system interface
    edit "port1"
        set allowaccess ping https ssh
    next
end

use_cases.title: Self-inflicted lockout
use_cases.situation: allowaccess was replaced instead of extended.
